The tarka (Quechua and Aymara: tharqa) is a wooden vertical flute of the Andean indigenous peoples, H-S 421.221.12. Usually of wood, it has six fingerholes, a fipple at the mouthpiece end and a free hole at the far end; it is shorter than a recorder and angular in shape, needs more air and has a dark, penetrating timbre. It comes in large, medium and small sizes, the medium and small pitched a fifth and an octave above the large; several often play the melody together in a large ensemble, accompanied by percussion such as the tinya and the wankar, a genre known as the tarqueada.

土土那琴的琴身主要採用非洲傳統硬木製成，包括共鳴箱與鍵盤框架。琴弦通常由天然纖維: The body of the tuntuna is made mainly of traditional African hardwoods, both the soundbox and the frame of the keyboard. The strings are usually of natural fibre or animal gut, which gives a warm timbre. Inside the soundbox, carefully chosen woods are used to strengthen the resonance. The keyboard mechanism may include wooden keys and metal linkages. Makers in some regions also use leather for decoration or protection, and the workmanship as a whole combines traditional design with practical use.
土土那琴起源於非洲撒哈拉以南地區，特別是西非和中非的傳統文化中。這種古老的弦樂器: The tuntuna originates in sub-Saharan Africa, in the traditional cultures of West and Central Africa in particular. This old stringed instrument, with its distinctive resonance and deep cultural roots, holds an important place in local communities. Its history is closely bound up with traditional African music, and it plays an indispensable part in tribal ritual, religious celebration and everyday entertainment.
土土那琴音色溫潤而富有穿透力，具有明亮的高頻特性與深沉的低頻共鳴。其音域寬廣，跨: The tuntuna's timbre is warm and penetrating, with bright high frequencies and a deep low resonance. Its range is wide, spanning several octaves, and it can render many layers of music. When the strings are struck the soundbox resonates warmly, which gives the sound a soft, full quality. The upper register has a clear metallic edge, while the lower register shows a solid wooden depth. Compared with the piano the tuntuna has more local character and more warmth; compared with the harp its sound is more concentrated and powerful. The vibration of the strings is amplified by a complex resonating structure, so that each note fills the space as a complete body of sound. Taken as a whole, the tuntuna has both the flavour of a traditional instrument and the expressive power of a modern one.

In the twentieth century, with the international spread of African music, the tuntuna gradually entered European and American musical circles. Ethnomusicologists and musicians began to study and promote the instrument, and it became an important representative of world music. Today the tuntuna is a musical bridge across cultural boundaries, and it is more and more widely recognised in music education and performance around the world.
